title: Lakshmana's anger
hookLine: the loyal younger brother says out loud what everyone is thinking, and offers to fight the whole city
carry: dharma can pull two ways at once
tomorrow: fate or effort: will Lakshmana fight?
last: SITA-RAM: NEVER ONE WITHOUT THE OTHER.

cards: We've watched Rama be calm for days. Valmiki makes sure we know not everyone is. When Rama told his mother the news, Lakshmana stood silent in the room.
Then, while Kausalya wept, he spoke, and out came the question the story has been holding back. This is wrong. Somebody should stop it.

teach.b: Valmiki lets us hear every layer of Lakshmana's anger. First, fairness. Rama has done nothing wrong; who in the whole kingdom can name a single fault in him?
To throw him out for no reason is against dharma itself. Second, the king.

teach.h: THE KING ISN'T FIT TO JUDGE.
teach.b: Lakshmana says what no one else will: the old man has been ruled by his desire for a young wife, and isn't fit to judge.
He goes further still, with words against his own father that Valmiki records and we won't repeat here. Third, action. I'm armed, he tells Rama.
I'm with you. If anyone in this city takes Bharata's side, I'll fight them all. Every word comes from love for his brother, and Hindu tradition remembers Lakshmana for that devotion.

teach.h: LISTEN TO YOUR BROTHER. DON'T GO.
teach.b: Listen to your brother, she tells Rama. Don't go. Now look at what just happened.
Lakshmana isn't arguing against dharma. He's arguing from it.

teach.h: PROTECT THE INNOCENT, OR KEEP THE WORD?
teach.b: A prince's duty is to protect, and an innocent man is being thrown out.

teach.h: DHARMA CAN PULL TWO WAYS AT ONCE.
teach.b: Rama will answer from dharma too: a son keeps his father's word. Both brothers are good, and dharma is pulling them in opposite directions. Hindu teachers have an old phrase for this: dharma is subtle.
It isn't a rulebook you look things up in. Sometimes two real duties collide, and loyal people stand on both sides. So where do you look?
The old Hindu law books name three places: scripture, the example of good people, and, in the end, your own conscience. That's still how many Hindu families weigh a hard choice.
Tomorrow, what Rama does with his brother's argument.

how: Hindu tradition remembers Lakshmana for a brother's devotion; in this outburst he argues from dharma, a protector's duty to the innocent, against Rama's dharma of keeping a father's word. 'Dharma is subtle' is the old phrase for such collisions. Where duties collide, the law books point to scripture, the conduct of good people, and one's own conscience.

o: Rama's father, the old king of Ayodhya
Rama's loyal younger brother, ready to fight for him
the general who guards Dasharatha's palace

p: offers to fight the whole city
begs Rama to listen to his brother
not fit to judge, Lakshmana says

s: he argues from it: exiling a man with no fault is against dharma itself, he says.
Kausalya sides with Lakshmana at first
she begs Rama to listen to his brother and stay.
Lakshmana's anger is aimed at Rama
it all comes from love for Rama; it's aimed at the injustice.

games.q: you're Lakshmana. your brother has just been stripped of his kingdom for no fault. what do you do?
o: stay silent; it's not my place.
say it's wrong, and offer to fight for him.
games.why: he speaks up: Rama has done no wrong, the king isn't fit to judge, and he'll fight anyone who takes Bharata's side.

practice: Remember a time you were angry on someone else's behalf, and let a little of that heat come back. Notice where it lives: chest, hands, face. Then ask what duty it was defending: fairness, family, a friend.
On each breath out, hold that duty gently next to the other one in the room, the one someone else was keeping. Picture a good person you trust standing between them: what would they see?
If you pray, ask for the clarity to see both.

wordCard.voice: Lakshmana, Rama's loyal younger brother. Loyal to the bone, he says Rama has done no wrong and offers to fight the whole city for him.

orig.note: Sanskrit lakṣmaṇa: the name of Rama's younger brother, Sumitra's son, who stands beside him through the exile.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: dharma can pull two ways at once. Lakshmana isn't finished. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 21 (Lakshmana's outburst in Kausalya's rooms; Kausalya's plea)
